open-question.question: Where the single wait is the dispatch call's own blocking form, how does the orchestrator wait for a repaired return sent as a continuation message to the held agent session, which is not a dispatch: the continuation is sent in the same blocking form, repairs are re-dispatched fresh so the blocking form applies, or repaired returns fall to per-wake-up batching?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: On the host whose single wait is the dispatch call's blocking form, the continuation tool has no blocking form, a send resumes the held agent and its end arrives later as a delivered message, so a repair that keeps the agent's context cannot be waited for in one call there, and the per-wake-up rule the goal already writes is the wait that exists; a fresh blocking re-dispatch would redo the whole analysis instead of a re-emit from intact context and reverse the goal's continuation-first order on the one host where continuation works; the conditional form adds an arm no current host meets; deferring one batch until the whole repair set has landed saves shell calls but not wake-ups and leaves finished repairs uncommitted meanwhile; refusals have been rare since the tool took over extraction, so the extra wake-ups cost little.
open-question.alternative: Repairs stay continuation-first in the blocking-dispatch arm. Every continuation from one refused batch is sent without blocking in the same turn, and each later wake-up that brings repaired-return notifications triggers a batch over whatever has landed in the scratch directory. This is the same rule the no-blocking arm uses for all its returns. Any fresh re-dispatch fallback is sent the same way. It keeps the goal's continuation-first repair and reuses the existing per-wake-up batching rule without inventing a new wait. It works on Claude Code as the tools stand, since a resumed agent's end already arrives as a notification and the batch input scan already picks up any file that arrived after the last batch. A run with refusals no longer wakes once, which the single-wait arm exists to ensure. It can take one batch call and one orchestrator turn per wake-up across the repair set, and repaired returns that land in separate notification groups are embedded in separate shell calls.

The repair branch order stays as it is: continuation first, fresh re-dispatch only where the session cannot be continued or its handle is gone. The waiting sentence for the blocking-dispatch arm gets a second capability condition. Where the host's continuation message also has a blocking form, every repair continuation from one refused batch goes out in one message in that form, and the orchestrator runs one more batch over the repair set once that message returns. Where it has no blocking form, the continuations are sent without blocking, and the repaired returns are batched in whichever wake-ups they arrive in, as in the no-blocking arm. It keeps the goal's continuation-first repair, which reuses the agent's context instead of redoing its analysis. It is also written in the same capability-conditional style as the recorded Claude Code wait, so a host that later gains a blocking continuation gets the single wait without a wording change. On Claude Code the continuation tool takes no blocking parameter. A send resumes the held agent, and its end arrives later as a notification, so the first arm never fires there. The sentence then carries a condition no current host meets, and in practice the run ends with per-wake-up batching for repairs.

Where the host's continuation message has a blocking form, the repair continuations from one refused batch are sent together in that form, and one batch follows when the message returns. Where it has none but dispatch can block, as on Claude Code, the repairs skip continuation and are re-dispatched fresh. Each repair is one blocking dispatch with the original prompt plus the corrective message, all in one message, followed by one batch over the repair set. Per-wake-up batching is never used in the blocking-dispatch arm. Every wait in the blocking arm stays a single blocking call, whatever the host's continuation tool offers. The orchestrator wakes exactly once per repair round and never processes repaired returns one wake-up at a time. On Claude Code every repair redoes the full analysis, at about 3.8k output tokens per agent, instead of re-emitting from intact context. This reverses the goal's "continuation where the host can" order for that host, and the recorded repair-rounds decision, both of which make the fresh dispatch the fallback, not the default.

The blocking-dispatch arm drops the continuation branch with no condition. Every repair from one refused batch is a fresh blocking dispatch with the original prompt plus the corrective message, all sent in one message, and one more batch runs over the repair set when that message returns. The per-wake-up arm keeps continuation first. It is the simplest wording: the blocking arm has one repair mechanism and one wait shape, without a second capability test to state or check. The repaired returns arrive by the same mechanism the first returns did. It pays the re-analysis cost on every repair and departs from the goal's continuation-first repair on exactly the host where continuation works. It also makes the repair branch's choice depend on the waiting arm, which couples two parts of step 3 that are separate today.

alternative.id: Continuation, one batch after the whole repair set

open-question.alternative: Repairs stay continuation-first and are sent without blocking, all in the same turn. The orchestrator knows which titles it sent repairs for, so it lets wake-ups pass without a batch call until every repaired title's agent has ended, with `DONE` or `FAILED`. It then runs one batch over the whole repair set in one shell call. The repair round is embedded and committed in exactly one shell call, the same shape as the first wait-and-batch, and continuation still preserves the agents' context, so neither the batching shape nor the repair cost is given up. The orchestrator must track the open repair titles in its context and still spends a turn on every wake-up that brings part of the set, so it saves shell calls but not wake-up turns. A repaired agent that never notifies holds the repair batch indefinitely unless the wait-expiry handling covers this wait too.

open-question.question: On a host that dispatches in cap-sized rounds, does a round's repair set get its own wait-and-batch before the next round is dispatched, or do the repairs ride in the next round's wait beside that round's first dispatches, counting against the cap?
open-question.recommendation: It applies the repair-rounds decision's one more wait-and-batch over the repair set to Codex unchanged, where a wait_agent call on the repair set alone is exactly that call; each batch then holds one kind of return and every round starts at the full cap, so the Codex value needs no cap arithmetic and no last-round rule; the extra wake-up falls only on a round with a refusal, which the tool's extraction has made rare, whereas riding the next round holds a finished repair uncommitted behind the slowest first dispatch and the overlapped form pays two waits for an earlier commit of returns the batch would embed anyway.
open-question.alternative: On a host that dispatches in cap-sized rounds, each round's repair set gets its own wait-and-batch before the next round goes out. As soon as a round's batch call refuses some returns, the orchestrator closes that round's accepted and skipped agents with `close_agent`. It sends every repair together in the same turn, as a continuation to each held session or as one fresh re-dispatch per question. It then waits in one `wait_agent` call on the repair set alone and runs one more batch over the repaired files. Only after that does it close the repaired agents and dispatch the next round at the full cap. A round with no refusals goes straight to the next round. The repairs never share a wait with first dispatches, and they never take a slot from the next round. It applies the recorded rule for blocking-wait hosts ("one more wait-and-batch over the repair set") to Codex unchanged. Every round's pipeline finishes before the next round starts. Each wait covers one kind of return. Every new round gets the full cap. So the Codex wording needs no cap arithmetic and no mixing of repaired and first returns within one batch. Every round with even one refusal costs one more orchestrator wake-up and one more batch call. While the repair wait runs, every slot except the repaired agents' sits idle, so wall-clock time grows by about one repair turnaround per such round. A milestone with several refusals spread over several rounds pays this several times.

The repairs do not get a wait of their own. When a round's batch call refuses some returns, the orchestrator closes the round's accepted and skipped agents and keeps the refused agents' sessions open. In the same turn it sends every repair and dispatches the next round's first agents. Because the held or re-dispatched repair agents count against the cap, the next round's new dispatches number the cap minus the repair set's size. One `wait_agent` call then covers the repairs and the new dispatches together, and one batch call embeds everything that landed. The orchestrator tells repaired titles from first returns because it sent the repairs itself, so a repaired return refused again goes straight to the per-question skip. The last round's repairs have no next round to join, so they get one closing wait-and-batch of their own. Repairs cost no extra wake-up and no extra batch call except after the last round. No slot sits idle waiting on a short repair while questions are still pending. This keeps the number of orchestrator turns per run, the main thing this milestone exists to cut, at one per round. Each next round shrinks by the number of repairs, and the Codex wording needs that cap arithmetic plus a rule for the last round. A quick repaired return also waits for the slowest first dispatch of the next round before it is embedded, so its commit lands later. If the run is interrupted during that wait, a repair that already finished is left uncommitted.

The repairs run alongside the next round but are waited on separately. When a round's batch call refuses some returns, the orchestrator closes the round's finished agents. In the same turn it sends every repair and dispatches the next round into the remaining slots, the cap minus the repair set's size, so the repairs count against the cap. It then waits in one `wait_agent` call on the repair set alone and batches the repaired files. After that it closes the repaired agents and waits in a second call on the round's first dispatches, followed by that round's batch. The last round's repairs get the same first wait with no new dispatches beside them. No slot sits idle during a repair, as in riding the next round. Repaired returns are still embedded and committed as soon as they land, not after the slowest first dispatch. So an interruption loses less finished work, and each batch call still holds only one kind of return. A round that follows refusals costs two wake-ups and two batch calls, the extra turn that riding the next round avoids. The Codex wording also needs both the cap arithmetic and the two-wait sequence. That makes it the longest value of the three, for a gain that is only an earlier commit of returns the batch would have embedded anyway.

open-question.question: What does the one batch shell call print so the orchestrator can tell which questions embed refused and with which Error line, given that embed prints nothing on success and the call pipes several files: each file's Short Title ahead of its embed output, only the refused titles each paired with its Error line, or nothing beyond the tool's own stderr?
open-question.recommendation: The orchestrator needs exactly the refused titles, each paired with the Error line that fills its repair message and, after a second refusal, its advisory entry, and every success is already recorded by its own commit, so printing it buys nothing and grows the orchestrator's context with the question count instead of the refusal count; tool stderr alone cannot pair two Error lines with their titles, so a repair would carry another question's reason; the companion file adds a write and a naming rule for a record nothing reads back, since the advisory is printed in the same run.
open-question.alternative: The batch call prints one line per file that `embed --alternatives` refused: that file's Short Title, taken from the file name, then a separator, then the `Error:` line the tool printed for it. A question that embedded prints nothing, and git's output for successful commits is silenced. A commit that fails is printed the same way: its title, then git's error. If every file embedded and committed, the call prints nothing. The output is exactly what the next step needs. Each line already pairs a refused question with the `Error:` line that fills its repair template and, after a second refusal, its step-4 advisory entry. The cost in context scales with the number of refusals, not the number of questions, and a clean batch prints nothing, the same way a successful `embed` does today. A successful embed and commit is never confirmed on the console. The orchestrator assumes success from silence, so a wrong redirect or a broken loop that never runs `embed` looks the same as a clean batch. The orchestrator also has to write the loop that captures and pairs each `embed` call's stderr correctly in the one shell command.

For each file it pipes, the batch call prints that file's Short Title, taken from the file name, on its own line. Below the title it prints whatever that title's `embed --alternatives` and commit printed: nothing from `embed` on success, or its one `Error:` line on refusal, followed by git's own commit output when the embed wrote. Successes are printed as well as refusals. The orchestrator finds a refused question by seeing which title has an `Error:` line under it, and a failed commit shows up in the same place as git's error. Every outcome can be traced from the output. Each piped title appears whether it embedded, was refused, or failed at commit time, so nothing the batch did is hidden, including a failed commit. The orchestrator can also check the print against the files it knows it dispatched. The output grows with the number of questions, not the number of problems. Every success adds a title line and git's commit lines to the orchestrator's context on each batch, which works against the token savings this milestone exists for. The orchestrator also has to read through all of it to find the few titles that carry an `Error:` line.

alternative.id: Refused pairs printed and kept on disk

open-question.alternative: The batch call prints the same pairs as the refused-only option: for each refused file, its Short Title, then a separator, then its `Error:` line, with successes and successful commits silent. In the same call, it also writes each refused file's `Error:` line into a companion file beside the refused return in the processed subdirectory. That companion file is named for the Short Title, so the refusal and the reason it was refused are kept together on disk in the run's scratch directory. It keeps the batch-input decision's principle that the record lives on disk rather than in the orchestrator's context. The reasons for the step-4 advisory and the refused returns they explain can be re-read from the scratch directory after many wake-ups. Because cleanup deletes nothing, a refused return and its reason stay available to inspect together. It adds a second write per refusal and a second file-naming rule to the runner's prose and the batch command. That extra mechanism buys little, because the orchestrator still has to read the printed line to send the repair at once. The advisory is printed in the same run, so nothing actually needs the record on disk.

The batch call adds nothing of its own. Its output is only what the tool and git print: no titles at all, and an `Error:` line on stderr for each refused file, in the order the files were piped. The orchestrator works out which questions were refused afterwards, with a follow-up `list --without-alternatives` call: the blocks still without alternatives are the refused ones. When a single line was printed, it is matched to the single refused title. The batch command stays as simple as possible, with no formatting or pairing logic in the runner's prose. That leaves less shell code for a runner to rewrite wrongly, and it relies only on the tool's existing contract, which the goal leaves unchanged. Most of `embed`'s fragment errors do not name the question, so when two or more files are refused in one batch, their `Error:` lines cannot be matched to titles. The repair message then loses its aim, or must carry an error line that may belong to another question. It also costs a second call, so the batch is no longer the one call that tells the orchestrator what happened.
